diversity contraction across substrates
Diversity contraction across substrates refers to how the variety, richness, or genetic/semantic diversity of a system shrinks, plateaus, or collapses depending on the physical or conceptual foundation (substrate) it grows or relies upon.
Depending on the context—whether microbial ecology, genetic range contraction, or semantic/cultural theory—this manifests in specific ways:
1. Microbial Ecology & Growth Substrates
Recalcitrant vs. Labile Substrates: Microbial communities behave differently under disturbance depending on whether they grow on complex carbon sources (like cellulose) or simple ones (like glucose). 

National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
 +1
Diversity Peaks: Cellulose-grown communities often peak in diversity at intermediate disturbance frequencies, whereas glucose-grown communities tend to peak under high competition or maximum disturbance through distinct competitive exclusions. 

National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
Physical Substrate Complexity: Microbes and macroinvertebrates form higher species richness and Shannon-Wiener diversity on rough, grooved, or porous physical substrates (such as treated concrete or silica) compared to smooth or artificial surfaces like microplastics. 
2. Genetic & Biological Range Contraction
Shrinkage vs. Fragmentation: When species experience range contraction, the pattern (core shrinkage, peripheral amputation, or habitat fragmentation) dictates the loss of genetic diversity. 

National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
Nucleotide Loss: Habitat fragmentation causes the steepest drop in nucleotide diversity (>50%) and builds strong genetic differentiation, whereas core shrinkage maintains local diversity longer. 

National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
Speed of Contraction: Paradoxically, fast-paced range contractions can sometimes preserve higher local genetic diversity in refugia than slow, lingering contractions. 

Oxford Academic
3. Semantic & Theoretical Exhaustion ("Diversity Contraction Across Substrates")
The Boundary Law: In theoretical models (such as works by Lee Sharks et al.), diversity contracts into a permanent low-diversity "trap" when natural regeneration vanishes faster than pruning near zero (D → 0), unless an exogenous novelty floor exists. 
The Mediation Ratchet: As systems rely more heavily on model-mediated or synthetic generation while unmediated human/natural diversity declines, the baseline "floor" can become disconnected from real meaning-reproduction channels, leading to semantic exhaustion or quarantine states. 
Are you looking at microbial communities, ecological genetics, or the theoretical semantic framework? Let me know which direction you want to explore further.
